name: Ecdysterone

lead: Ecdysterone (20-hydroxyecdysone) is the molting hormone of insects and crustaceans, also found in plants such as spinach and Cyanotis. Lifters take it as a plant-derived anabolic, with some promoting it as a hormone-neutral way to add muscle and a bigger physique.

In rodents it stimulates muscle protein synthesis without androgen receptor activity, with evidence pointing to estrogen receptor beta and Akt signalling. A 2019 controlled study funded by the World Anti-Doping Agency reported larger gains in muscle mass and bench press with ecdysterone alongside training, while a 2006 study found no significant effect on training adaptations. Replication is sparse.

paras: Sold as capsules or powder and taken daily alongside a normal training and protein routine over several weeks. It is also being developed as an investigational compound for muscle conditions.
Acute toxicity appears low. It is sold as a supplement, though the World Anti-Doping Agency has monitored it. Product purity is reported to vary, and long-term human safety has not been established.

angle.text: Lifters take ecdysterone as a plant-derived anabolic to add muscle on top of training, some describing it as hormone-neutral. One controlled human study reported larger gains in muscle mass and bench press with it, and cell and animal work points to estrogen receptor beta. Product quality is a recurring concern.

lead: Ecdysterone, formally 20-hydroxyecdysone (20E), is a naturally occurring steroid hormone that controls molting and metamorphosis in insects and crustaceans. Plants such as Cyanotis, Ajuga turkestanica and Rhaponticum carthamoides also make it, where it is thought to defend against herbivores; spinach and quinoa contain smaller amounts [1][2][3].

People take it as an over-the-counter supplement in the hope of building muscle, strength and recovery that show up in the mirror. The chain is: supplement taken alongside resistance training, claimed greater muscle protein synthesis and training adaptation, more lean mass and a fuller physique. It is often sold alone or stacked with other plant-based products such as turkesterone, laxogenin, ashwagandha and tongkat ali [4][5][6][7][3].

Mammals lack the arthropod ecdysone receptor, but ecdysterone still acts on mammalian systems; hypotheses include estrogen receptor beta and, in developer literature, the Mas1 receptor [1][8][9]. Human research includes a 2006 study reporting no significant effect of an oral amount on training adaptations, a 2019 controlled study funded by the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) reporting larger increases in muscle mass and bench press performance with ecdysterone, and a 2025 12-week randomised trial of a commercial 20E-containing product [1][10][11]. It is also being developed by a pharmaceutical company as an investigational compound for muscle and metabolic conditions [9].
WADA added ecdysterone to its monitoring programme in 2020, a step noted as controversial because spinach and quinoa contain the compound [3].
infobox: Insects and crustaceans; Cyanotis, Ajuga turkestanica, Rhaponticum carthamoides, spinach, quinoa [1][3]
Dietary supplement (US, OTC); investigational drug candidate [1][9]

paras: Ecdysterone is marketed in bodybuilding supplements. Wikipedia says it is sold for bodybuilding, and a 2024 review states that ecdysteroid supplements are widely marketed, mostly to athletes, partly because they can be isolated from high-yielding plants at competitive cost [1][3]. T Nation members describe adding it to pre-workouts and stacks alongside ashwagandha, tongkat ali, fadogia, laxogenin and turkesterone [4][5][6][7], and some report that it made a 'noteworthy difference' in strength, recovery, body fat and well-being in combination with other products [4]. A 2021 poster recommends only 'proper products with standardized contents' [12]. Another suggests it as a way to lower estrogen effects instead of raising testosterone, warning of underdosed supplements [13].

In 2001 a T Nation thread proposed a forum experiment to test ecdysterone, asking supporters to supply numbers [14]. In 2007 a user described smoking a suma root powder containing 2 percent ecdysterone as an experiment [15]. On looksmax.org, a thread titled for ecdysterone drew jokes about how much users had spent on it [16].

Turkesterone is a related phytoecdysteroid found in Ajuga turkestanica and other plants; Wikipedia says it is under laboratory research for possible anabolic effects, possibly via PI3K and AKT signalling, and that its pharmacokinetics and human effects are undetermined [17]. Wikipedia's ecdysteroid article notes online sellers market Ajuga turkestanica extracts as bodybuilding supplements and states they are not approved as drugs in any country [18]. The 2024 Nutrients review covers ecdysterone and turkesterone together [2][3].

Registered trials include 20E in sarcopenia (NCT03452488), in prediabetes (NCT03906201), in giardiasis (NCT04827537), and in patients with obesity starting semaglutide to assess muscle wasting (NCT07411378) [19][20][21][22]. Wikipedia notes the FDA approved a study of 20E in obesity in 2024, focused on lower-limb muscle strength, named in its source as Biophytis's phase II study [1]. A 2021 developer-authored review describes the pharmaceutical-grade form BIO101 and a 26-week sarcopenia trial in adults aged 65 and over, and a COVID-19 pneumonia trial [9].

Wikipedia's ecdysteroid article describes arthropods making ecdysteroids from dietary cholesterol, and plants producing phytoecdysteroids mostly as defences against insect herbivores [18]. The 2021 review says 20E was identified in arthropods and in plants in 1965, that Cyanotis roots are the main commercial source, and that Rhaponticum, Serratula, Pfaffia and Achyranthes also accumulate it [9]. The 2024 Nutrients review reports Rhaponticum carthamoides root content of roughly 0.05 to 1.7 percent, quinoa seeds with several-fold more 20E per dry weight than spinach leaves, and wide variation in spinach levels [3]. That review notes the contrast between the amounts athletes are advised to take and the amounts obtained from food, since even a kilogram of spinach rarely supplies as much as supplement doses [3].

A 2006 study found that an oral amount did not significantly change anabolic or catabolic responses, body composition or training adaptations [1]. A 2019 controlled clinical trial in Archives of Toxicology, funded by WADA, reported significantly greater increases in muscle mass and one-repetition bench press in participants given ecdysterone, with a dose-responsive effect [1][10]. A 2025 12-week randomised double-blind training study tested a commercial phytosteroid product containing 20E and diosgenin and examined the reliability of its labelling [11]. A 2024 review covers ecdysterone and turkesterone in sport [2].

The 2024 review describes further human work: a 10-week study of 46 men using a commercial ecdysone supplement that reported increases in body weight, muscle mass and strength with no adverse effects and no change in steroid profile; an 8-week trial in resistance-trained men that showed no change in training adaptation; and a phase 1 trial in healthy young and older adults in which the compound was well tolerated. The authors state that multicentre randomised double-blind trials are still needed and that the mechanism of action remains unclear [3]. Animal studies mostly suggest anabolic effects, though a study in 20-month-old mice found no change in muscle mass [3].
Grokipedia summarises human trials as mixed and attributes some null results to commercial supplements containing far less 20E than labelled [23]; this is from an AI-generated source.

The 2024 review describes ecdysteroids as generally considered safe in mammals, citing very high oral LD50 values in mice and no obvious adverse responses in rats over three months, while noting one study of a Rhaponticum preparation that reported cytogenotoxic activity [3]. The 2021 developer review reports no serious adverse events in single- and multiple-dose human studies and no genotoxicity in rats and dogs [9]. Long-term human safety in supplement users has not been established in the literature cited. Forum users caution about underdosed supplements and recommend standardised products [12][13].

In arthropods 20E acts through the ecdysone receptor [1]. In mammals, a 2014 study reported that estrogen receptor beta is involved in skeletal muscle hypertrophy induced by ecdysterone [8], and the WADA-funded human study's abstract states that the anabolic effect is thought to be mediated by estrogen receptor binding [10]. Wikipedia describes relatively selective activation of ERbeta in human muscle cells and also lists it as a MAS1 agonist [1]. The developer review's leading hypothesis is activation of the Mas1 receptor in the renin-angiotensin system, with ERbeta as an alternative, and the authors say the mechanism is still uncertain [9]. Grokipedia adds activation of PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathways [23].
Research on other effects includes bone regeneration via BMP-2/SMAD/RUNX2 signalling and protection of rat liver mitochondria under immobilisation stress, both preclinical [24][25].

Wikipedia notes high oral bioavailability in animals [1], whereas the 2021 review reports low oral bioavailability of about 1 percent in the cited work and extensive metabolism, partly by gut bacteria [9]. Studies have examined urinary excretion of ecdysterone and its metabolites after spinach consumption and possible dietary sources of ecdysterone in urine, relevant to anti-doping interpretation [26][27].

Ecdysteroid research began with insect hormones; Grokipedia states 20E was first isolated from the silk moth in the 1960s [23], and the 2021 review says 20E was identified in arthropods and plants in 1965 [9]. Early interest was in insect control, and pharmaceutical research, much of it in Eastern Europe, followed; commercial supply of pure 20E later enabled wider study [9]. The 2024 review says Rhaponticum carthamoides received extensive research attention in Russian sport and was widely used by Soviet and Russian elite athletes, and that Brekhman and Dardymov classified it as an adaptogen in 1969 [3].

Studies in Drosophila in the 1970s and 1980s used ecdysterone to study gene induction and heat-shock responses [28]. Wikipedia describes use of ecdysteroids as inducers in transgenic animals as a research tool [1]. In supplement culture, a 2001 T Nation thread already debated whether ecdysterone 'works' [14]. WADA added it to its monitoring programme in 2020 [3].

Human trials of ecdysterone for muscle: a 2006 study [1], the 2019 WADA-funded study [10], and the 2025 12-week trial of a 20E and diosgenin product [11]. Reviews: ecdysterone and turkesterone in sport and nutrition [2][3] and degenerative diseases [29], and a developer-authored review of clinical use [9].
Registered trials listed above cover sarcopenia, prediabetes, giardiasis and obesity with semaglutide [19][20][21][22].

lore.intro: On T Nation ecdysterone has been a subject of debate since the early 2000s and is now typically mentioned as an add-on supplement, with repeated cautions about product quality [14][12][13].
